title: Seitan: protein, carbs, and nutrition explained

seo.title: Seitan: protein, carbs, calories, and nutrition
seo.meta_description: Seitan is hydrated cooked wheat gluten. Many products provide 20–30 g protein and roughly 130–180 calories per 100 g, but carbs and sodium vary widely.
seo.search_intent: Understand what seitan is, how much protein and carbohydrate it contains, and why nutrition labels vary so much by product.

excerpt: Seitan is essentially cooked, hydrated wheat gluten. That lets it pack roughly 20–30 grams of protein into 100 grams with little fat, but there is no universal seitan number: water, starch, broth, and seasoning can move the label substantially.
content_html:
Seitan is often described as a meat substitute, but nutritionally it is something more specific: hydrated wheat gluten that has been shaped and cooked, usually with broth, soy sauce, spices, or other ingredients.

How much protein does seitan have?

Prepared products vary, but roughly 20–30 g protein per 100 g is common. One FoodData Central branded reference works out to about 141 calories, 24.7 g protein, 5.9 g carbohydrate, and 2.4 g fat per 100 g.

Wetter products can land near 20 g protein while dense recipes can exceed 30 g. Do not compare dry vital wheat gluten powder directly with cooked seitan: the dry ingredient contains dramatically less water.

Seitan still contains carbohydrate

A simple seitan can contain only about 5–10 g carbohydrate per 100 g, but flour, starch, sugar, or sauces can raise that number. A product with 25 g protein and 6 g carbs is not the same food profile as one with 20 g protein and 15 g carbs even if both say seitan on the front.

Fat is usually low until the recipe adds it

Without substantial added oil, prepared seitan can fall around 1–3 g fat per 100 g. Pan-frying or an oily marinade changes the meal quickly: 10 g absorbed oil adds about 90 calories.

Sodium deserves a close look

Wheat gluten itself does not require a high sodium level, but seitan is often simmered in salty broth or seasoned with soy sauce. Commercial products can therefore range from a few hundred milligrams to 700 mg sodium or more per 100 g.

Is seitan a complete protein?

Wheat protein contains all nine indispensable amino acids, but lysine is relatively limiting compared with the human reference pattern. That does not make seitan useless; it means protein quality reflects the whole amino-acid supply across the diet.

Beans, lentils, and soy are comparatively lysine-rich and can complement wheat-based foods across meals without requiring a precise combination at every sitting.

Seitan is not gluten-free

The main ingredient is gluten itself. Seitan is not appropriate for people with celiac disease or for anyone who has been medically advised to avoid wheat or gluten.

Micronutrients vary more than the headline protein number

Iron, phosphorus, selenium, and B vitamins depend on the wheat, recipe, and fortification. Vitamin B12 should never be assumed; ordinary seitan provides meaningful B12 only when a B12-containing ingredient is added or the product is fortified.

The useful takeaway

Seitan can be a very concentrated plant-protein food with little intrinsic fat, but the nutrition label matters. Compare prepared products per 100 g or per equal serving and pay attention to protein, carbs, fat, and sodium.

faq.question: How much protein is in seitan?
faq.answer: Many prepared products provide about 20–30 g per 100 g; one FoodData Central branded example is about 24.7 g per 100 g.

faq.question: Does seitan have carbs?
faq.answer: Yes. Simple products may be around 5–10 g per 100 g, while recipes with starch, flour, sugar, or sauces can be higher.

faq.question: Is seitan gluten-free?
faq.answer: No. Seitan is made primarily from wheat gluten and is not suitable for celiac disease.
